episode_title: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek

stories.topic: Bastiat Spent His Last Breath on His Ideas
stories.summary: Frédéric Bastiat, the 19th-century French writer, economist and parliamentarian, died at 49, the age Amit was when recording. He caught tuberculosis while travelling around France popularising his ideas. Knowing his lungs were failing, and referring to his book The Law, he wrote that he would proclaim his principle with all the force of his lungs, which were all too inadequate. Joseph Schumpeter called him the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived.
stories.insight: Bastiat was explaining ideas like opportunity cost before the terms were in common use. His early death leaves you wondering what he would have written with more time.
stories.quote: Until the day of my death I shall proclaim this principle with all the force of my lungs, which alas is all too inadequate.

stories.summary: Amit was the first person to win the Bastiat Prize twice. The prize goes to journalists who promote the values of a free society. Tim Harford later won it twice as well. The trophy is a candlestick, a nod to Bastiat's satirical Candlemakers' Petition, in which candlemakers ask the government to block out the sun.
stories.insight: The trophy carries the joke of its namesake's most famous satire, so the argument against protectionism sits on Amit's shelf.
stories.quote: So I have two candlesticks at home among my most prized possessions, though I'm not one for material goods really, but they just symbolize that to me.

stories.topic: Earthquake Bread at Four Times the Price
stories.summary: As a student in the early-to-mid 90s, Amit volunteered after an earthquake in Gujarat and rode in an ambulance with paramedics. In one village almost every building had collapsed, but a couple of shops were open and had raised the price of bread three or four times. His first reaction was that this was evil. Later he understood that the high price stopped the first family from buying up all the bread. Families could pool money so everyone got a few slices.
stories.insight: In a crisis, moral intuition and economic logic can point in opposite directions. 'Gouging' prices ration a scarce good so it gets shared, while a capped price lets the first comer take everything.
stories.quote: And my instant thought at that moment was that, oh man, this is evil. This is just freaking evil.

stories.topic: The Friend Who Missed His Flight
stories.summary: About three years before the recording, the AAP government in Delhi tried a price cap on Uber, just a day before a friend of Amit's needed to get to the airport. With surge pricing gone, no cab was available and the friend missed his flight.
stories.insight: A price cap doesn't remove scarcity. It turns the scarcity into missing supply, and the person with an urgent need is the one left stranded.
stories.quote: And the guy could just simply could not get a cab to go to the airport and he missed his flight.

stories.topic: Predicting That the Stent Price Cap Would Kill
stories.summary: When the Indian government capped the price of stents because they were 'too expensive', Amit tweeted (or wrote in a column) that the cap would cause shortages and people would die. He says that is exactly what happened.
stories.insight: Economic first principles let you predict outcomes. 'Price controls always lead to shortages' is a forecast you can make in advance, not just an argument.
stories.quote: this is going to lead to shortages, people are going to die. Exactly that happened.

stories.topic: Raj Narain, Indira Gandhi and the Government Jeeps
stories.summary: Ajay recalls that Raj Narain took Indira Gandhi to Justice Sinha's courtroom in the Allahabad High Court over the 'sweet little problem' of using government jeeps for campaigning. Because the Congress party and the government were legally separate, her election was invalidated. That was India in 1975.
stories.insight: Separating party from state is a real protection, not a technicality. Ajay contrasts it with China, where party and state are the same thing.
stories.quote: That there's a separation. There is the Congress party and there is the government. The government owns Jeeps. When you use the government Jeeps for the purpose of campaigning, that is not on, and your election is invalidated, and that's what India was at in 1975.

stories.topic: How China's Makers Learned to Serve the Party
stories.summary: Ajay describes China in stages. First there was some real promise that founders could build businesses fairly. Then, again and again, party-connected 'takers' used state power to push innovators into distress sales or shut them down. Capitalists got the message: over the last 15 years, any significant business needs party members on the board or a 'princeling' (a child of party leaders) as a shareholder. That protection comes with unpredictable future demands, from 'give this guy a job' to 'run your product differently'. The result is a regime of uncodified taxation, as before the Magna Carta, and an investment slump. Russia is one step further, where Putin decides whether an oligarch is jailed, exiled or murdered.
stories.insight: Owning wealth means little unless it can stand up to the state. Entrepreneurs who agree to the 'fixing' are not thinking two moves ahead.
stories.quote: So a government that will give you anything that you want is a government that can take away everything that you have.

stories.topic: Jeff Bezos Takes On Donald Trump
stories.summary: To offset the gloom about China and Russia, Ajay points to Jeff Bezos, who made his fortune building Amazon and bought the Washington Post. The Post did investigative journalism going after Donald Trump, and the President and the federal government could not shut it down or hit back at Bezos. In Russia, Ajay says, a billionaire who owns a critical newspaper would 'experience some accidents' and 'fall out of a window'.
stories.insight: What keeps a society free is whether its institutions constrain the most powerful office, not whether its leaders are kind.
stories.quote: And it is a tribute to that country that the office of the president and the federal government was unable to do anything about it, was unable to shut down the Washington Post, was unable to hit back at Jeff Bezos.

stories.topic: Who Is the Greatest Human of the Last 30 Years?
stories.summary: Amit sometimes asks people who has had the greatest positive impact on humanity in the last 30 years. His own top candidate was Jeff Bezos, until a friend argued for Deng Xiaoping, who lifted hundreds of millions of Chinese out of poverty. Ajay answers Ken Thompson, the main inventor of Unix. On Deng, Ajay quotes Zhou Enlai: 'it's too soon to tell'. His reason is that the intra-party democracy and term limits Deng built have peeled away.
stories.insight: Your answer shows what you value most: consumer value, mass escape from poverty, or the invisible infrastructure of computing.
stories.quote: My answer would be Ken Thompson... Ken Thompson is main inventor of Unix. And you know, we didn't start the fire, Ken did.

stories.topic: The Economist Who Sneered at Hazlitt Readers
stories.summary: Amit recalls an economist both hosts know, one who had defended demonetisation or at least urged a wait-and-watch approach. This economist complained that too many people arguing with him had only read Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson. Amit's reaction was that this is enough, because those readers have the first principles.
stories.insight: Knowing basic economics thoroughly beats credentials that ignore it. Amit's comparison: you wouldn't trust a physicist who doesn't believe in gravity.
stories.quote: And I'm like, That's enough. Those people know more than you, right? They know the first principles.

recommendations.item: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Introduced as the essay that inspired the name of Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen; it opens with the parable of the broken window.
recommendations.reason: It teaches you to look past a policy's visible effect to its unseen costs, the core habit of a good economist.

recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Amit reads out Bastiat's passage on the origin of property versus the origin of plunder.
recommendations.reason: Amit says every paragraph carries wisdom and power, and it is a strikingly modern lens for looking at India. It is free to read.

recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Cited as the home of Bastiat's satirical petitions, including the one to ban everyone from working with their right hand.
recommendations.reason: Bastiat could boil complex ideas down to stories anyone understands, showing how absurd protectionism and the 'more work equals more prosperity' fallacy are.

recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Discussed as Bastiat's satire in which candlemakers ask France's rulers to block out the sun to protect their livelihoods; it is why the Bastiat Prize trophy is a candlestick.
recommendations.reason: Taking protectionist logic seriously leads straight to an absurdity, and once you've laughed at it you can't take 'save local businesses' rhetoric at face value.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's reply to Oscar Lange's proposal for a central price committee.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it the most important and seminal essay of the twentieth century. It explains how the price system, not central planning, coordinates an economy.

recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it while explaining Hayek's two-part insight on dispersed information and price coordination.
recommendations.reason: It argues that the knowledge society needs is spread across everyone, so a planner will always get it wrong. Ajay says the computer revolution keeps reviving that conceit.

recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Mentioned while recommending everything by the two Freddies; Amit had recommended it in a previous episode.
recommendations.reason: Hayek can be heavy going, and Butler's primer is a friendly way in.

recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: Brought up after Adam Smith's 'man of system'; Amit says it's an essay he wants everyone to read.
recommendations.reason: A pencil narrates how its parts come from many countries, made by people who never talk to each other. Prices do the coordinating, a small everyday miracle of spontaneous order.

recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Leonard Read's essay.
recommendations.reason: A filmed version of the pencil parable for those who prefer watching to reading.

recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Mentioned while explaining spontaneous order in cities, economies and language.
recommendations.reason: It shows how much of the world (language, economies, even natural selection) evolves without a designer.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Amit mentions his early episode with Ridley on the book.
recommendations.reason: A long-form conversation about how order emerges without central design.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Raised as the answer to the watchmaker argument against natural selection; Ajay adds the example of the eye.
recommendations.reason: The greatest marvels of nature need no planner, the biological version of Hayek's point about economies.

recommendations.item: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Mentioned during Amit's critique of counting government spending in GDP.
recommendations.reason: A deep look at what GDP can and cannot measure, and the problems with how the number is built.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Show-notes companion to Amit's argument, illustrated with tariffs on teddy bears, that most interventions redistribute from the poor to the rich.
recommendations.reason: Sets out in writing the episode's central claim that the redistribution runs opposite to the stated intention.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit says he'll link his columns on price controls while discussing stents, cars and Uber.
recommendations.reason: The written version of the argument that you cannot legislate scarcity away.

recommendations.creator: Jan-Werner Müller
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a great book on populism while discussing how simplistic narratives win power.
recommendations.reason: Helps you recognise how populists work. Amit adds that the most important ingredient is simplistic narratives.

recommendations.item: Why Both Modi and Trump are Textbook Populists
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions he wrote a column on Müller's ideas, then uses Trump's 2016 'China bad, foreigners taking your jobs' story as the example.
recommendations.reason: Applies the framework to two contemporary leaders and shows how slogan-sized stories crowd out complex truths.

recommendations.creator: Elias Canetti
recommendations.context: Ajay calls it a great book while discussing how political actors use rage and simple-minded economics to gain power.
recommendations.reason: Useful for understanding how anger gets mobilised into an 'us vs them' route to power.

recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Used to refute the zero-sum view of the world: buying a coffee, both buyer and seller say thank you.
recommendations.reason: A simple illustration that voluntary exchange is positive-sum, with both sides better off.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the episode; Amit calls it a masterpiece.
recommendations.reason: Not an introductory book, but Ajay says each chapter was 'like an earthquake' that shakes you and makes you think about the world.

recommendations.creator: Milton and Rose Friedman
recommendations.context: Recommended alongside Capitalism and Freedom; Amit notes it also became a TV series, possibly on YouTube.
recommendations.reason: Another Friedman classic on voluntary exchange. Amit uses it to make his point that capitalism equals consent and is the opposite of cronyism.

recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: Amit's main recommendation for the episode, a book inspired by Bastiat's essay on the seen and the unseen.
recommendations.reason: It uses basic principles to clear up misconceptions about price controls, tariffs and inflation. It has sold over a million copies in some 40-50 languages, and Amit thinks everyone should study economics because it is the study of human behaviour.

recommendations.item: Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek (economics rap battle)
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the episode's discussion of Hayek.
recommendations.reason: A fun way into the Keynes–Hayek debate that Ajay says the 20th century settled against central planning.

recommendations.item: Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek (Economics Rap Battle Round Two)
recommendations.context: Show-notes sequel to the first rap battle.
recommendations.reason: Round two of the same playful take on the great debate.

core_ideas.concept: The Seen and the Unseen (the Broken Window)
core_ideas.explanation: A boy breaks a window and people say it's good for the economy because the glazier gets paid. What is unseen is what the owner would have done with that money, such as buying a coat or a cake. The same fallacy drives claims that war is good for the economy. Unintended effects are often foreseeable once you understand economic laws.
core_ideas.quote: Because a bad economist will only look at your first order effect. But a good economist will take everything into account and will consider those principles seriously.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit objects to counting government spending in GDP, an argument he says Keynes and others won before the Second World War. The government could tax people to dig ditches and fill them, and GDP would rise without anyone being better off. A flawed number that becomes a target can be gamed.
core_ideas.quote: And every metric can be gamed.

core_ideas.concept: Unintended Consequences and the Implausibility of Conspiracies
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay credits Robert K. Merton (1936) with the idea that all purposeful social action has unintended consequences, because cause and effect are subtle, nonlinear and only dimly understood. Karl Popper takes this further. If even 20 people struggle to achieve a goal together, conspiracy theories that require many secret actors to land a ball in a distant hole are hard to believe.
core_ideas.quote: That the world will surprise us, and we only dimly understand the full consequences of all-purposive social action.

core_ideas.explanation: Populists and nationalists gain power by selling simple-minded economics that turns poor people's anger against elites. Trump's 2016 story about lost jobs ('China bad', 'foreigners are taking your jobs') was appealing and mostly false. The real causes were many and complex, and a complex story can't become a slogan.
core_ideas.quote: That complex story is hard to get across. You can't make a slogan out of it, but you can make a slogan out of a simple story, right?

core_ideas.concept: Interventions Redistribute From the Poor to the Rich
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's teddy-bear example: a tariff of 20 rupees pushes a 90-rupee Chinese bear to 110, so consumers buy the local 100-rupee bear. Ten rupees per buyer moves from consumers to local manufacturers, who also lose the incentive to improve. Public choice theory calls this diffuse costs and concentrated benefits: each consumer barely notices the loss, while an organised lobby collects the gain.
core_ideas.quote: But most government interventions in the economy, in the market, if not all, redistribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.concept: Why States Prefer Tariffs to Blowing Up the Railroad
core_ideas.explanation: Bastiat's satirical 'negative railroad' and a tariff have the same effect on consumers. Ajay's public-choice point is that blowing up a railroad or a port is a one-time decision. A tariff is discretionary: it can be granted, removed or reintroduced industry by industry. That hangs a sword of Damocles over the business class, which must keep funding those in power. Amit adds that following incentives explains party positions, such as AAP opposing FDI in retail because small retailers are among its biggest supporters.
core_ideas.quote: So what is the one thing better than redistributing from the poor to the rich? The answer is achieving Godlike power over the entrepreneurial class to boot.

core_ideas.explanation: Bastiat: you can prosper by applying your own faculties (property) or by seizing what others produce (plunder). Today plunder usually runs through the coercive power of the state, as rent-seeking and cronyism. People choose whichever path is less burdensome. When the state makes honest trade too hard, as in India's early decades, a rent-seeking mentality takes hold.
core_ideas.quote: If it is easier to seek profit, you will seek profit. If it is easier to seek rent, if seeking profit is really hard, then you will seek rent.

core_ideas.concept: Makers vs. Takers, and the Price of Refuge
core_ideas.explanation: Makers build products and organisations that serve consumers. Takers grab what others built, and once the state has a monopoly on violence, they do it through regulations and rules. Protection from the state comes with unpredictable demands later, which is in effect unpredictable taxation. So Ajay argues businesspeople must think philosophically about capital allocation and risk.
core_ideas.quote: Every form of refuge has a price.

core_ideas.concept: Counterfactual Histories as a Thinking Tool
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay suggests imagining going back in a time machine to advise Deng Xiaoping in 1978, or Nehru. These were people who meant well and tried to see the future, yet went wrong in many ways. Asking what you'd tell them sharpens your understanding of how the world works.
core_ideas.quote: But these are very useful levers and tools for us to play these counterfactual histories. Because they help us to clarify our insights into the world.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues from a Maslow-style hierarchy that safety and freedom come first and prosperity second, so Deng's achievement is questionable when most people in China lack that safety. He also points to Putin's Russia, an economy propped up by oil. Amit pushes back: safety and freedom partly come from having the means to secure them, so escaping poverty has value in itself.
core_ideas.quote: The most fundamental thing that human beings want is that sense of safety.

core_ideas.explanation: Many beautiful things are, in Adam Ferguson's phrase, the product of human action but not human design. Bastiat's example is how Paris gets fed with no committee. Cities, languages and natural selection work the same way. Ajay prefers the mathematical term 'self-organising system': local decisions, no central control, remarkable results. The world should be a process of discovery, not design.
core_ideas.quote: So the fundamental fact remains that we should let the world be a process of discovery, not design.

core_ideas.concept: Hayek's Knowledge Problem and Price Coordination
core_ideas.explanation: Knowledge about preferences and circumstances (your need for a taxi, a driver's willingness to work) is spread across society, so no planner can know it all. Prices coordinate everyone without anyone needing to talk. Ajay calls the price system the heart and soul of economics, to the point of wanting COVID vaccines traded on free markets with futures contracts.
core_ideas.quote: We just let the prices do it. The entire dance of the market economy is organized by prices, and we don't need to talk to each other, we just look at the prices, and everything happens.

core_ideas.concept: Prices Carry Information and Incentives (Uber Surge Pricing)
core_ideas.explanation: Say 200 people want cabs and only 20 are available. Under a price cap, the first 20 get them, even if they're casually heading to the mall while someone else needs a hospital. Surge pricing does two things. First, it lets those who value the ride most pay for it. Second, and more important, it signals an idle driver to come out and earn by serving others, which adds supply.
core_ideas.quote: So the price carried information, the price carried an incentive, and more and more cabs get on the street because they want to make money

core_ideas.concept: Price Controls Always Lead to Shortages
core_ideas.explanation: If cars were capped at ten thousand rupees, existing cars would be snapped up and production would stop. The same logic applies to stents, Uber rides and earthquake bread. A cap doesn't change how scarce something is. It just removes the mechanism that rations it and calls forth more supply.
core_ideas.quote: So people simply don't realize that you cannot legislate scarcity away.

core_ideas.concept: The Fatal Conceit Returns With Computers (and the Man of System)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says the 20th century taught one bumper-sticker lesson: central planning brings stagnation, because people, not bureaucrats, are the source of innovation. Computers and AI keep reviving the planner's dream, a game of whack-a-mole. Amit links this to Adam Smith's 'man of system', who imagines he can move people like pieces on a chessboard. Ajay's counter is that humans are already intelligent agents acting on local knowledge.
core_ideas.quote: Okay, we are all AGIs that are walking this planet trying to do things for ourselves.

core_ideas.explanation: Capitalism is many people acting voluntarily in positive-sum exchanges, the 'double thank you moment' where buyer and seller each value what they get more than what they give. It is often confused with cronyism, its opposite. What is good for markets is not what is good for big businesses.
core_ideas.quote: If you're for consent, you are for capitalism because it's a voluntary action of people making each other better off.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Producer Vartika's T-shirt line about Karjat, where the episode was recorded: 'Badi Badi Baatein, Wada Pao Khaate' (big talk while eating vada pav). Amit says it seems targeted at the two of them, and that Karjat has the best vada pav in the world.

The episode is framed around Amit's 'friend Freddie', who must be kept in the frame and is named after his two heroes, Frédéric Bastiat and Friedrich Hayek. During his teddy-bear tariff example Amit adds, 'No one is better than my Freddy.' At the end he suggests Milton Friedman could be a Freddy too 'if you twist his surname around a bit.'
Ajay on conspiracy theories: 'conspiracy theories are the opiate of the asses', because to believe one 'you have to be simple-minded.'

Bastiat's satires as Amit retells them: candlemakers petitioning to block out the sun, a petition to ban everyone from working with their right hand (since more effort supposedly means more prosperity), and the 'negative railroad' solution to foreign competition: destroy the railroads.
Amit on GDP: with government spending counted, you can keep 'digging up ditches, filling them, digging up ditches, filling them, and the GDP is just growing and growing.'
Asked about Deng Xiaoping's legacy, Ajay quotes Zhou Enlai: 'it's too soon to tell.'
Ajay names Ken Thompson, main inventor of Unix, as the greatest human of the last 30 years, riffing on the song line: 'we didn't start the fire, Ken did.'
Ajay explains that prices spare us explicit coordination ('you will play Hamlet and I will play Ophelia'). Amit replies: 'if you ever play Ophelia, I will be happy to play Hamlet. But don't blush.'
Ajay, after Amit says Bastiat died at 49, Amit's own age: 'you have fifty more years to go... you owe the world five big books in your next fifty years.'

Ajay voices a pragmatic Chinese entrepreneur cutting deals with the party: 'Chodo yaar, I have to get three party people as my board members. I'll do it... Anyway, I keep my 80%, no?' The fixing has been done. Meanwhile, a Russian billionaire who owns a critical newspaper 'will just experience some accidents, you'll fall out of a window.'

Amit on armchair economists: everybody gives gyan on economics, though nobody would give gyan on nuclear physics without studying it. And 'a physicist who does not believe in gravity is not a physicist I would trust.'
The sign-off: 'Please like and subscribe. It's a voluntary action. Double thank you moment if you've watched so far.'
Joseph Schumpeter called Bastiat 'the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived'.
Jagdish Bhagwati once said the Chinese were turning out to be profit-seeking while Indians were rent-seeking. Amit says he doesn't know enough about China to judge, but it rings true for India.

Oscar Lange's proposal for a central price committee was what Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' argued against. Amit links it back to Bastiat's essay on how Paris gets fed without any central committee.
Adam Ferguson's phrase 'the product of human action but not human design', and Adam Smith's 'man of system' who treats society like a chessboard.

The watchmaker argument against natural selection, answered by Dawkins' The Blind Watchmaker. Ajay notes that the eye is more wonderful than any wristwatch found on a beach, yet has no designer. Amit also nods to Dennett and Pinker.

Daniel Pipes' Property and Freedom, discussed in the previous episode, is invoked on whether a country's wealth can stand up to the state. Ajay compares China and Russia to the world before the Magna Carta, when the king could make arbitrary, uncodified demands.
Ajay calls himself part of the 19th-century tradition of economics, closer to the dreams of Ricardo, Adam Smith and Marx, and finds today's economics 'a pale shadow of what it can be.'
